title: Did police fail Bobby Ramroop? Why a Toronto man's family has been left with anguish - and hauntingly familiar questions
subtitle: After talking to the officers who were trying to help him, the 32-year-old climbed out a window and fell 16 storeys. His family is suing the Toronto police
article: Framed photos and poster boards line Debbie Indal's apartment.

Her son, Taresh Ramroop, smiles back from most of them - in a red cap and gown after graduating from Seneca College; in his purple and black FedEx uniform; as a small boy in a white dress shirt and belted slacks.

But Ramroop, whose family lovingly calls him Bobby, is not here. The bedroom, the one with the window he climbed out of and fell 16 storeys, is now home to piles of orange bottles for the pills that help Indal cope with post-traumatic stress.
Indal pulls back the dark curtain in front of the window to show the sliding pane of glass that opens to leave a gap exactly 21.7 inches wide.

That fact, one of many devastating details of Ramroop's death, is detailed in the report from the director of the police watchdog that cleared of wrongdoing the Toronto police officers who responded to the apartment that day.

Now, his mother, Indal, and sister, Vanessa Persaud, are suing Toronto police, alleging officers failed to adequately respond to the mental health crisis their 32-year-old son and brother was having on a day in October 2022.
"My son's death was senseless," Indal tells the Star. "The police failed him."

What the Special Investigations Unit's report doesn't reflect is the unending anguish of Ramroop's family - how Indal won't make her son's favourite turkey dish again; how bystander videos of his death haunt them still.

For all its details and analysis, what the report doesn't talk about is the unanswered questions left for families when people die after interactions with the police. They are questions the city has yet to fully grapple with after several high-profile incidents. Why were heavily armed tactical officers called in? Why didn't police let Ramroop's mother speak to him, even when he was begging to hear her voice "one last time"?
His mother believes that, had they been allowed to come inside her own apartment that day, to say, "'Bobby, Mommy home,'" things could have been different.
"He would have opened the door and come out. Bobby would have been here today," Indal said, sobbing.
Ramroop was born in Guyana on Nov. 1, 1989, and immigrated to the GTA with his mom at age three.
He was shy, Indal says, never wanting to walk beside her. She would carry him on her hip and he would hide in the aisles of the stores she carted him to in Brampton.
Eventually, they settled in the Jane Street and Finch Avenue area, where he attended public school before he was accepted to Seneca College.

As an adult, Ramroop helped provide for his single mother, whom he lived with in the Finch Avenue apartment alongside his brother after his sister moved out. He took two jobs - working in the distribution centre at FedEx and delivering UberEats by foot.
"The day he passed away, he went to FreshCo across the street with a neighbour," his sister, Persaud, recalled. "He held all her bags for her and walked upstairs with them."
Ramroop's family is honest about the fact he struggled with his mental health. But he was never violent, they say.

He attended church across the street on Sundays and was working on a graphic design to celebrate his community - bold letters declaring it "Finchtown" that his family has now turned into T-shirts and other memorabilia.

That afternoon, Indal was in the middle of her first day back at her hotel job after pandemic lockdowns when she got a call from her son she couldn't answer. Then came a message she didn't understand: Someone is burning down the house, her son said. When she tried to call him back, he didn't answer. She said she thought maybe he had been confused, just smelled someone cooking, and had since decided to nap after work.
As she was taking the bus home, her neighbour called and asked what was going on. Police officers were crowding the hallway outside her apartment. Indal said she was almost home.
When she arrived, she saw papers and clothing littering the ground outside her complex.

Around 4:30 p.m., three people had called 911 about someone throwing items from the top floor of the building, landing on the fenced-in playground outside the daycare housed in the base of the building, according to a report from SIU director Joseph Martino.
A dispatcher sent several police officers to the building and notified the police's specially trained and rifle-armed Emergency Task Force, which also arrived on scene.

The dispatcher told officers that, earlier that day, an "emotionally disturbed person" had called 911 and was acting "paranoid." Martino, in his report, said Ramroop had complained about someone breaking into his apartment and hearing "silent noises" before hanging up.
Uniformed officers entered the apartment using a key from the building's superintendent just before 5 p.m., the report said.

For half an hour, officers tried to talk to Ramroop through his closed bedroom door. At one point, the SIU report says, Ramroop told officers he wanted them to shoot him. Officers heard what they believed to be furniture being stacked against the door. One officer canvassed the apartment kitchen where they found a knife block that was missing a knife. Ramroop's brother was home when officers arrived and wasn't aware of the distress his brother was in, the statement of claim said. He told officers the knife might have been in the wash, the SIU report said.

Meanwhile, as Indal entered the building's lobby - followed later by Persaud and her husband - police corralled them in the superintendent's office on the main floor. They kept them there for hours, their statement of claim says. Police would not let them speak to Ramroop, the women said, telling them not to call or text him.
Meanwhile, ETF officers wearing tactical gear and carrying their weapons, took over negotiating with Ramroop from the uniformed officers who were first responders, the statement said.

According to the SIU report, officers told Ramroop they were concerned about the items being thrown and that they couldn't leave until he came out. At one point, they drilled a hole in his bedroom door to pass him juice and get eyes on him inside his bedroom.
At several points, Ramroop seemed confused and paranoid about who the officers were, asking to see their badge and saying he wanted to call the police.
Several times, he asked the officers to speak with his mom.
"I want to talk to her one last time," he told the officers.
"One last time and what happens then, man?" an officer responded, according to a transcript of audio detailed in the SIU report.
The report notes that bystanders who had gathered below were "chirping" Ramroop, telling him to jump. An officer told him not to listen to them.
"You're forcing me to jump, bro," Ramroop told the officers, at one point.
Starting at 6:40 p.m., the SIU report said Ramroop became "increasingly reckless."
He was climbing in and out of his room, "sometimes hanging out the window." An officer who was stationed at the neighbouring window pleaded with him to go back inside.
Twice he hung from his windowsill, but pulled himself back up.
The third time, he lost his grip.
The statement of claim said it was hours after his fall before police told his family, waiting in the office downstairs, what had happened.
When they were finally brought out of the office, Indal recalls seeing an ambulance outside. Maybe, she thought, they were going to take her son to the hospital.
She looked at the officer speaking to her, but could not believe the words coming from her lips: "Deceased."
"Where was the help?" Indal cried as she recounted the story. "Where was the help for my son?"
In 2000, Toronto police, after public outcry over incidents of people in crisis being killed by or dying in the presence of police officers, created mobile crisis intervention teams.
The teams, which have since expanded to 16 policing divisions, pair a specially trained uniformed police officer with a mental health nurse to respond to emergency calls for someone in crisis.

The teams have been criticized by some for continuing to advance a police-centric approach to crisis calls while proving ineffective in situations like the one at Ramroop's apartment. Because police won't dispatch the teams to calls for unknown trouble or possible weapons calls, they have not been present at various high-profile deaths since their inception.
Martino, the SIU director, wrote in the report concerning Ramroop's death that the mobile crisis team was not a "viable option given the possibility that a knife was in play."

In the wake of the 2020 death of Toronto woman Regis Korchinski-Paquet, who fell to her death from her family's apartment balcony after police were called to the building for a domestic disturbance, advocates rallied for more non-police supports for people in crisis (Martino also cleared police of any wrongdoing in that case).
In January 2022, several months before Ramroop's death, the city unveiled a new civilian-led community crisis service.

But the teams of trained crisis workers, which are expected to expand citywide by the end of this year, the city has said, are limited to calls without threats of weapons or violence - which would disqualify them from being dispatched to help in situations like Ramroop's.
Ramroop, police would come to learn, was never armed.

"It was, or should have been, clear from the earliest involvement of the TPS that this was a mental health and not a criminal matter," reads the statement of claim filed on behalf of Ramroop's mother and sister from a team at Toronto law firm Waddell Phillips.
"Instead, the TPS created, escalated and prolonged a stand-off with Bobby that lasted approximately two hours."

Sandy Hudson, co-founder of Black Lives Matter Canada and author of the forthcoming book Defund: Black Lives, Policing and Safety For All, said governments have yet to "step up and do what needs to be done for public safety."

"There is no reason why this sort of outcome should be repeating itself over and over when everyone from politicians to experts have acknowledged that this is the wrong outcome," she said in an interview.
She argues that the "number one solution" is to "remove power from police in responding to these incidents."
"My question is what is it going to take to do what is so obviously clearly needed in taking this responsibility away from police officers?"
In a detailed statement following the incident, then Toronto police chief James Ramer, offered his sympathies to Ramroop's family while explaining the police response.

He said instances of "barricading" automatically require "a higher level of response," according to police procedures "given the elevated risk of harm" and that deploying a mobile crisis team was not possible.

Additionally, he explained that there was never any direct confrontation with Ramroop and that ETF officers, two of whom were certified crisis negotiators, also requested an on-call psychiatrist to attend but that they did not arrive before Ramroop fell.

In the SIU report, Martino addressed the issue of having a family member intervene with a person in crisis, saying it must be approached on a case-by-case basis and that it can "trigger an impulsive or fateful reaction." Given Ramroop's state of mind, Martino wrote, he was unable to fault the decisions police made that day.
Ramer added that police co-operated fully with the SIU investigation, including providing video and audio recordings from officers' body-worn cameras.
Sitting in her apartment without her son, Indal has another question, one that feels impossible to answer.
She doesn't want anyone else to feel the pain her family has.
"Would anything change in the future?"
